data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A century ago, people removed one animal from Yellowstone because they saw it as a pest. The whole landscape changed in ways nobody expected. Today you learn why pulling one thread moves the whole web.

1. Read **Pull One Thread** — the wolf story at the end is true.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Bingo** round.
3. Study the **Web Roles** chart — every living thing has a job.
4. Sort the organisms in **What's Your Job?**
5. Take the quiz — question 4 asks you to predict a chain reaction.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to explain a food web in your own words.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Web** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Investigation: What Would Happen If…?** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Big idea to carry: in an ecosystem there is no such thing as doing only one thing. 🐺🌲

objectives.label: I named three living things from my own neighborhood and their roles

history.title: Pull One Thread
history.data:
## Pull One Thread

Every living thing has to get energy from somewhere. Follow that energy far enough back and it always ends in the same place: sunlight.

**Producers** make their own food. Plants, algae, and some bacteria capture sunlight and build sugar. Everything else on Earth is a customer.

**Consumers** eat other living things. Herbivores like deer and grasshoppers eat producers. Carnivores like hawks and wolves eat other consumers. Omnivores like bears and humans do both. Each step is a **trophic level** — a rung on the energy ladder.

**Decomposers** get the least attention and do the most essential work. Fungi, bacteria, and worms break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste. That releases nutrients back into the soil, where producers can use them again.

Without decomposers, an ecosystem would bury itself in its own dead material. The nutrients would never get back into circulation, and everything would starve.

A **food chain** is one straight path: grass → grasshopper → mouse → hawk. Real nature almost never works that neatly. A hawk eats mice, snakes, and rabbits. A mouse eats seeds, insects, and berries. When you draw all those connections at once, you get a **food web**, and a web behaves very differently from a chain.

Here is the part worth remembering: energy leaks. Only about **ten percent** of the energy at one level makes it to the next. The rest gets spent on moving, breathing, and staying warm. Much of it escapes as heat.

That one fact explains a lot. A meadow can support thousands of grasshoppers, hundreds of mice, and only a couple of hawks. Big predators are rare because the energy math will not support more of them.

Now the thread-pulling. Wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone by the 1920s. Without them, elk populations grew and grazed heavily along rivers, stripping young willows and aspens. Beavers lost their building material. Songbirds lost nesting cover. Riverbanks eroded without roots holding the soil.

Wolves were reintroduced in 1995, and much of that reversed. Willows recovered in places. Beavers returned. Some riverbanks stabilized.

Scientists still argue about how much of this the wolves caused directly. Weather and bear populations mattered too. Ecosystems are complicated, and honest scientists debate the details.

But the core lesson is not in dispute: **you cannot remove one species and change only one thing.**

data.title: Remember the Web
data.instructions: Three sets of facts from Pull One Thread. Study the example aid for each, then make your own and explain how it connects back to the science.
data.sourceExcerpt: Producers make their own food. Consumers eat other living things. Decomposers break down dead plants, dead animals, and waste. Only about ten percent of the energy at one level makes it to the next. You cannot remove one species and change only one thing.

cards.target: The three roles: producer, consumer, decomposer
essentialFacts: Producers (plants, algae, some bacteria) make their own food from sunlight.
Consumers eat other living things: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both.
Decomposers (fungi, bacteria, worms) break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
cards.aiExample: P-C-D: Plants Cook Dinner. Producers cook it from sunlight, Consumers eat it, Decomposers clean up.
cards.mapping: The three letters follow the order energy travels: it is made (P), eaten (C), and finally recycled (D). The kitchen picture keeps each job separate.
scaffoldSteps: Write the three roles and circle P, C, D.
Pick a verb for each letter that matches the job: make, eat, break down.
Check that your sentence keeps the order energy moves.
coachPrompts: Which of your words shows that decomposers give nutrients BACK to producers?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own P-C-D sentence, or change the example so it sounds like you.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain how each word points back to what that role really does.

hookFact.text: Without decomposers, an ecosystem would bury itself in its own dead material and everything would starve.

cards.target: The 10% rule: only about a tenth of the energy moves up each level
essentialFacts: Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next level.
The rest is spent on moving, breathing, and staying warm, and much escapes as heat.
That is why a meadow supports thousands of grasshoppers, hundreds of mice, and only a few hawks.
cards.aiExample: Chunk it as a shrinking stack: 1,000 grass units, 100 grasshopper units, 10 mouse units, 1 hawk unit. Each floor of the stack is one tenth of the floor below.
cards.mapping: Grouping the numbers into a stack of tens turns 'energy leaks' into a shape you can see: wide at the bottom, one hawk at the top.
scaffoldSteps: Choose four organisms from one food chain, producer first.
Give the producer 1,000 units and divide by ten at each step.
Say why the top number is so small.
coachPrompts: Where did the other 900 units go at each step?
cards.studentPrompt: Build your own shrinking stack with organisms from a place you know.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your stack explain why big predators are rare?

hookFact.text: Big predators are rare because the energy math will not support more of them.

cards.target: Pull one thread and the whole web moves: the Yellowstone wolves
essentialFacts: Wolves were hunted out of Yellowstone by the 1920s.
Without wolves, elk grazed heavily along rivers and stripped young willows and aspens; beavers and songbirds lost what they needed and riverbanks eroded.
Wolves returned in 1995 and much of this reversed, though scientists still debate how much the wolves alone caused.
cards.aiExample: No wolves → more elk → bare riverbanks → no willow for beavers, no cover for songbirds → crumbling banks. Wolves back → fewer elk by the rivers → willows return → beavers and birds return → banks hold.
cards.mapping: Each arrow is one connection in the web. Reading the chain forward and backward shows the same species list moving in opposite directions, which is the lesson: no change happens alone.
scaffoldSteps: Start with the species that was removed.
Add one arrow for each thing that changed because of it.
Rewrite the chain with the species put back.
coachPrompts: Which link in your chain is the one scientists are least sure about?
cards.studentPrompt: Write a thread-pull chain for a species near where you live.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your chain show that removing one species changes more than one thing?

history.title: Systems Check

questions.question: Trace the energy in a hawk's body far enough back. Where did it originally come from?
options: The soil
The hawk's own body heat
The Sun
Water in the ecosystem

questions.question: Why does an ecosystem need decomposers?
options: They keep predator populations from growing too large
They make food from sunlight when plants cannot
They provide most of the energy for consumers
They return nutrients from dead material back to the soil for producers
questions.correctAnswer: They return nutrients from dead material back to the soil for producers

questions.question: Why are there far fewer hawks than grasshoppers in a meadow?
options: Only about 10% of energy passes to each higher level
Hawks reproduce only once every ten years
Grasshoppers are better at hiding than hawks
Hawks eat only plants, which are scarce
questions.correctAnswer: Only about 10% of energy passes to each higher level

questions.question: A disease wipes out most of the mice in a meadow. Predict the most likely chain reaction.
options: Nothing else changes, since only mice were affected
Hawk numbers drop and seed-eating insects may increase
Grass immediately dies without mice to eat it
Decomposers disappear because they only eat mice
questions.correctAnswer: Hawk numbers drop and seed-eating insects may increase

questions.question: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
options: A chain is for land and a web is for water
A web only includes producers and decomposers
There is no difference — they are two names for one thing
A chain shows one path; a web shows all the connections at once
questions.correctAnswer: A chain shows one path; a web shows all the connections at once

questions.question: Explain what happened in Yellowstone after wolves were removed, and what scientists still debate about it.
questions.expectedAnswer: Without wolves, elk grazed heavily along rivers and stripped young willows and aspens, which affected beavers, songbirds, and riverbank erosion. After wolves returned in 1995 much of this reversed. Scientists still debate how much of the change wolves caused directly versus other factors like weather and bears.

questions.question: Is a Venus flytrap a producer or a consumer? Defend your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: It is a producer, because it makes its own food by photosynthesis. It traps insects for extra nutrients like nitrogen in poor soil, not for energy — so it feeds like a plant and supplements like a consumer.

reflections.text: Pick one animal near where you live. What eats it, and what does it eat?
If humans disappeared from your local ecosystem tomorrow, name two things that would change.

items.text: If ____ disappeared from this ecosystem, then ____, and then ____.
A food web is different from a food chain because ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Ecologist |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roles | Names organisms only | Uses producer/consumer/decomposer | Uses all roles precisely, including trophic levels |
| Energy | Does not mention energy | Says energy moves | Explains energy loss and why predators are rare |
| Systems thinking | One-step effect | Two-step chain | Traces effects through 3+ connections in a web |

data.question: Do plants ever eat animals? 🪰
data.answer: A few, like the Venus flytrap, trap insects — but not for energy. They make their own food from sunlight like every producer, and use the insects for nutrients their poor soil lacks. Producer first, snack second.

data.question: Where do humans fit in a food web?
data.answer: We are omnivores, so we sit at more than one level: a salad puts us one step from producers, a burger two or three. Most of what we eat traces back to farmed plants, which are producers too.

data.question: What happens to all the energy that 'leaks'? ⚡
data.answer: It is used up keeping animals moving, warm, and alive, and most of it leaves as heat. It is not destroyed — it just is not available as food for the next level.

data.question: Are decomposers the same as scavengers?
data.answer: Close cousins. A vulture or a crab that eats a dead animal is a scavenger — a consumer. Decomposers like fungi and bacteria finish the job, breaking what is left all the way down into nutrients.

data.question: Could a food web survive without a top predator? 🐺
data.answer: It would keep existing, but it would change. Yellowstone showed that when wolves left, elk numbers grew and rivers, willows, beavers, and songbirds all shifted. The web reorganizes rather than disappears.

data.question: Why draw webs instead of chains if webs are messier?
data.answer: Because the mess is the truth. A chain hides the fact that a hawk has several foods, and that is exactly what lets it survive when one of them gets scarce. The web shows resilience; the chain hides it.

history.title: Investigation: What Would Happen If…?
history.meta: 5th Grade • Investigation brief • prediction with a web diagram

data.title: What Would Happen If…?
data.instructions: Pick one species in a local food web and investigate what would most likely change if it disappeared. Use lesson facts as anchors, mark your guesses as guesses, and build a prediction others can check.
data.fitReason: The lesson's core claim is that removing one species changes many things. An investigation asks students to make that claim testable for a web they can actually observe.

brief.context: A community group wants to remove a species from the park near your school because it is a nuisance: too many geese on the field, or too many deer eating the gardens, or the coyotes that have started appearing. Before anyone acts, they have asked for a student investigation of what else would change.
brief.drivingQuestion: If this one species were removed from the park's food web, what would most likely happen to at least three other living things there, and how confident can we be about each prediction?
brief.seedDirection: Draw the web first. Every arrow that touches your species is a place something could change.
lockedLessonFacts: Producers make their own food from sunlight; consumers eat other living things; decomposers return nutrients to the soil.
A food web shows all the feeding connections at once, and most animals eat more than one thing.
Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next, so predators are rare and depend on many prey.
Removing wolves from Yellowstone changed elk, willows, beavers, songbirds, and riverbanks; scientists still debate how much each change was due to wolves alone.
openQuestions: What does the chosen species eat, and what eats it, in THIS park?
Is there another species that would take over its role?
How would we know a year later whether our prediction was right?
stakeholders: The gardeners whose plants are eaten
The other species connected to the one being removed
Park staff who would do the removing
criteria: The web diagram shows at least six living things and every arrow is labeled as eats or is eaten by
At least three predicted changes each trace back through the web with a chain of arrows
Each prediction is marked as strong, likely, or unsure with a reason
At least four glossary words are used correctly
constraints: Predictions must use species that actually live in or near the park
No prediction may skip a link: every change needs the arrow that causes it
brief.deliverable: A labeled food-web diagram of the park with the chosen species highlighted, plus a written prediction of three changes, each rated for confidence and each explained through the web.

parallelExample.context: Fishers in one region removed most of the sea otters to protect shellfish.
parallelExample.move: Ecologists drew the otter's web first: otters eat urchins, urchins eat kelp, kelp shelters fish. They predicted that fewer otters would mean more urchins and less kelp, then watched the coast to check. The kelp forests vanished where otters were gone and returned where otters came back.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The same move: draw the web, follow the arrows two steps past the removed species, and state a prediction you can check later.

supports.frameStarter: If ____ disappeared from the park, then ____ would probably ____, because it ____.
frameChoices: Its prey would increase, and the things its prey eats would decrease
Its predators would lose a food source and might leave or decline
Another species would take over its role
Decomposers would have less to break down, changing the soil
coachPrompts: Which arrow in your diagram are you most sure about, and which one is a guess?
What did Yellowstone teach you about how confident to sound?
How would you check your prediction without removing anything?

data.coachHint: Two steps past the removed species is where the surprising changes live. Do not stop at one arrow.
